body.text: Why low pressure matters more here than the pressure itself

A lot of homeowners assume more pressure means a better clean, but on a wood deck the opposite is often true. High-pressure washing can etch grooves into softer boards, raise the grain unevenly and blow apart the fibres on pressure-treated pine in particular, since that wood is manufactured to be soft and easy to work with. Restore My Deck cleans at a controlled, low pressure and lets wood-safe detergents do most of the lifting, which gets dirt, algae and grime out of the grain without damaging the surface underneath. Cedar can tolerate slightly more pressure than pine, but we still favour the gentler approach across the board because it is the difference between a deck that looks clean and a deck that looks clean and stays structurally sound.
What Kitchener-Waterloo summers do to an uncleaned deck

Southwestern Ontario summers run humid, and that humidity is exactly what mildew, algae and mould need to establish themselves on a wood surface. A deck that sits shaded under mature trees, which describes a lot of yards in Kitchener, Waterloo, Cambridge and Guelph, tends to hold moisture longer after rain and is more prone to green or black staining by midsummer. Left alone, that buildup does more than look bad. It holds moisture against the wood fibres, which accelerates rot, and it creates a barrier that stops stain or sealant from bonding properly if you try to refinish over it. An annual clean interrupts that cycle before it becomes a bigger problem.
How cleaning sets up your deck for winter

Cleaning is not just about appearance heading into summer entertaining season; it is also the most important prep step before winter arrives. A clean, dry deck allows any stain or sealant applied in the fall to bond properly to the wood, which matters because that finish is what stands between your deck and months of snow load, ice and repeated freeze-thaw cycling. If dirt, mildew or old failing stain is left on the surface, a new coat applied over it will not adhere evenly and can peel or flake off well before spring, leaving bare wood exposed right when it needs protection the most.

body.text: Cleaning as a standalone service versus a prep step

Some homeowners book deck cleaning as a yearly maintenance habit on its own, particularly if the deck was stained or sealed within the last couple of years and just needs a refresh before summer. Others need it specifically as the first step before staining, sealing or a full restoration. Either way, we treat cleaning the same way: careful, low pressure, eco-friendly solutions, and a full rinse and dry-time check before we call the job finished. If your deck is due for more than a clean, /deck-staining and /deck-restoration pick up from there, and /deck-power-washing covers a slightly more aggressive approach for decks with heavier buildup or that can tolerate more pressure.
We recommend cleaning your deck at least once a year to keep it in good condition through Southwestern Ontario's humid summers and harsh winters.
Eco-friendly products, safe for families and pets

All the cleaning solutions we use are environmentally friendly and safe around kids, pets and garden plants near the deck. This matters in residential neighbourhoods across Kitchener-Waterloo where decks often back onto gardens, patios and play areas that get used the same day the work is done. We rinse thoroughly so nothing lingers on the surface or drains into the yard, and we schedule around forecasted rain so the cleaning solution has time to work before it gets washed away prematurely.

A lot of properties across Kitchener, Waterloo and Guelph have mature trees close to the deck, which is great for shade in July but tough on a wood surface. Overhanging trees drop sap, pollen and leaf debris that traps moisture against the boards, and shaded sections of a deck take noticeably longer to dry after rain than sections in full sun. We pay closer attention to those shaded, tree-covered areas during a clean, since they are usually where mildew and algae establish first and where dirt tends to build up fastest between visits.

faqs.q: Why use low pressure instead of standard power washing?
faqs.a: Low pressure combined with wood-safe detergents removes dirt and mildew effectively without etching or fuzzing softer woods like pressure-treated pine, which is more prone to damage under high pressure.

faqs.q: How often should I have my deck cleaned?
faqs.a: We recommend cleaning your deck at least once a year, both to maintain its appearance and to prepare it for winter conditions.

faqs.q: Will cleaning remove my old stain?
faqs.a: Cleaning will lighten and lift failing or worn stain, which is often exactly what is needed to prep the surface for a fresh coat, though it is not intended as a full stain-stripping process.

faqs.q: Is deck cleaning necessary before staining?
faqs.a: Yes. A clean, dry surface is essential for stain to adhere properly and last, so cleaning is always the first step before any staining or sealing project.

faqs.q: Are your cleaning products safe for pets and gardens?
faqs.a: Yes, we use eco-friendly, plant-safe solutions and rinse thoroughly, which makes the process safe for family, pets and nearby landscaping.

faqs.q: What does a deck cleaning cost?
faqs.a: Pressure washing and cleaning services typically run $800 to $1,200 depending on deck size, which we confirm with a free, no-obligation quote.
